result:
We still "dial" phones, though few people under thirty have ever turned a rotary dial. We "hang up," though there's no hook. We "cc" people on emails, invoking carbon paper, a product most office workers have never touched. Video is "footage" because film was once measured in feet, and we "roll down" car windows by pressing a button.

I love these fossils. Language keeps the shape of a tool long after the tool is gone, the way a dry riverbed keeps the shape of water. The save icon is a floppy disk, an object many people know only as the save icon. The symbol has outlived the thing it pictured.

What interests me is that nobody decides this. No committee voted to keep "dial." The word kept working, so it stayed, and its original meaning drained out while the function remained.

Most words turn out to be like this if you dig far enough. "Clue" once meant a ball of thread, the kind Theseus used to find his way out of the labyrinth. "Muscle" comes from the Latin for "little mouse," because a flexing bicep looked to someone like a mouse moving under skin. Every sentence we speak is paved with metaphors that someone once found vivid and that no one notices anymore.

So I wonder which of our current words are fossils in the making. "Scroll" already is one, twice over. "Streaming" probably will be. Someday a child will ask why a phone "rings" when phones haven't contained bells for decades. The honest answer will be the same as always: it worked, and nobody got around to stopping.
